raw_response.country: Multi-country / global (developing countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, plus the Netherlands)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community peri-urban water supply and sanitation service access in developing countries, including gaps in household connections to water and sewer networks, reliability, and affordability (Chapters 1 and 2).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 in its conceptual and illustrative discussions, though without primary empirical evaluation: under the plain wording, the edited volume broadly discusses institutional, governance, fiscal decentralisation, utility privatisation/concession, and regulatory factors; under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Chapter 1 discusses tariff and cost-recovery structures (flat, variable, block, connection, and lifeline charges, p. 10) and bureaucratic discretion (pp. 3, 21), while Chapter 2 discusses dwelling illegality, uncertain land tenure, and regulatory restrictions on irregular peri-urban settlements (such as Mexico City's Zero Growth Pact, pp. 40-42) that bar households from connecting to formal service networks. Under both readings, however, the record is excluded because it fails Criterion 3 (E05) and Criterion 5 as a non-empirical edited pedagogical textbook.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05): the record is a 13-chapter edited book originally developed to support a UNESCO-IHE distance-learning course and summer school for water professionals rather than an original empirical study or a systematic empirical synthesis. In the provided text (PDF pages 1-74 of 326; pages 75-326 truncated at byte limit), Chapter 1 is a conceptual/theoretical policy essay and Chapter 2 explicitly synthesises previously published reports (Allen et al. 2006, 2007, 2008) using illustrative case boxes. The complete front-matter inventories (Table of Contents, Lists of Boxes, Figures, and Tables) and Chapter 1.5's chapter-by-chapter overview likewise show a multi-topic collection of policy, historical, financing, benchmarking, and planning overviews/primers (with rural farming and agricultural wastewater-irrigation valuation tables in Chapters 9-10 unrelated to household water/sanitation access rules).
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses water and sanitation service access, network connection, reliability, affordability, and exclusion conceptually and via secondary literature examples, but reports no primary empirical access outcome estimates or systematic empirical synthesis findings.
criterion_notes.c5: As an edited 13-chapter pedagogical textbook spanning heterogeneous conceptual, policy, planning, agricultural, and methodological topics across multiple countries, the record lacks a single identifiable empirical study design, study population/sample, exposure, and measured service-access outcome (note: PDF pages 75-326 of 326 were truncated in the input text).

evidence_quotes.quote: More than 2.6 billion people in the developing world lack access to safe water and sanitation services (Rijsberman 2004).
In many cases, the illegality of their dwellings prevents the urban and peri-urban poor from connecting to formal systems of service provision or from using their homes as collateral.
Tariffs could also take the form of levies that support expansion of plant capacity through use of connection charges, facilities or capacity charge.
This collection of papers was initially developed to support a distance-learning course at UNESCO-IHE Institute for Water Education.

The empirical literature that supports the discussion is incipient but fast growing. Thus, the purpose is to highlight a number of case studies selected to aid the process of rethinking service delivery options and their governance implications

However, infrastructure coverage has not been matched by a growth in households connecting to water supply and sewer networks. Very often institutional factors made access to water supply connections by marginalised groups and households difficult.

raw_response.exposure: Conceptual and narrative discussion of institutional, governance, tariff/cost-recovery, co-production, and peri-urban land-tenure/legality frameworks
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (no empirical evidence). Record R975C44396921 (Kurian & McCarney, eds., 2010, DOI 10.1007/978-90-481-9425-4) is an entire 13-chapter edited pedagogical volume developed for a UNESCO-IHE distance-learning course on peri-urban water and sanitation policy, planning, and assessment methods. Although Chapters 1 and 2 conceptually discuss peri-urban water and sanitation service access (c1=yes) and rule-type mechanisms including connection tariffs/lifeline rates and tenure/legality barriers barring informal settlements from formal connections (c2=yes under both plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings), the volume as a whole is neither a primary empirical study of water/sanitation service access nor a systematic empirical synthesis (c3=no), and lacks a unified empirical study design, sample, exposure, and measured access outcome (c4=no, c5=no). Confidence is set to medium because PDF pages 75-326 of 326 were truncated by the input byte limit, though the complete front matter (Table of Contents, Lists of Boxes/Figures/Tables), complete Chapter 1 (including Section 1.5's summary of all chapters), and Chapter 2 pp. 27-42 (explicitly noting synthesis of prior reports Allen et al. 2006, 2007, 2008) establish the pedagogical overview nature of the book.
raw_response.study_design: Edited pedagogical book / narrative policy, planning, and methods collection (non-empirical)
